anomaly_def.Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Static mismatch between table structures / indexes and workload access patterns forces inefficient access paths.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: On-disk pages and index structures are internally inconsistent or corrupted, making logical structures unreliable.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: Underlying storage subsystem is saturated, causing high read/write latency and queueing regardless of database configuration.

When all three root causes are present, the database simultaneously executes poorly tuned access paths, encounters unpredictable data-corruption‐induced plan fallbacks, and faces physical I/O saturation. Typical symptoms include: pervasive full-table or full-index scans that already strain disks; sudden, erratic result-set discrepancies or duplicate/missing rows caused by corrupt indexes; optimizer unexpectedly abandoning indexes and reverting to table scans, further inflating I/O; skyrocketing wait times for data-file, temp, and log I/O; alternating spikes of CPU (from repeated re-execution after corruption errors) and long stretches of I/O wait; integrity-check or consistency-check operations running longer than normal and themselves throttling on storage bandwidth; and a flood of engine alerts ranging from checksum failures to "slow I/O" warnings, making problem isolation difficult.

Causally, a sub-optimal physical design magnifies the demand for disk access, pushing the storage layer toward its throughput limits. Corrupted index or data pages then force the optimizer or runtime to discard otherwise efficient index paths, escalating to even heavier full-scan patterns and random probing that intensify disk pressure. The already saturated storage in turn prolongs recovery, consistency-check, and rebuild operations, leaving corrupted structures in place longer and increasing the likelihood of further corruption during stressed I/O conditions. This positive feedback loop between poor design, physical corruption, and I/O bottlenecks degrades performance, erodes data reliability, and complicates remedial actions, as each anomaly both masks and amplifies the others.

entry.cause_analysis: The failure is typically associated with file creation, filesystem access, write durability, log persistence, tablespace management, or storage-capacity boundaries.
entry.solution_guidance: Inspect filesystem capacity and permissions, verify persistence paths, review log and data placement, and check whether storage latency or write failures are affecting the engine.
